feed.title: CSS & UI Kits — Useful Sites
feed.subtitle: A hand-curated, annotated link directory across ten areas, from software and AI to security, economics and architecture. Every entry states what the resource does and where it parts ways with its neighbours.

entry.title: Animista
entry.summary: A library of ready CSS animations you can play, tweak and copy the code from. Unlike adding a whole library such as animate.css, you take only the code for the animation you need.

entry.title: Autoprefixer
entry.summary: A tool that automatically adds browser prefixes (‑webkit‑, ‑moz‑) to CSS. Unlike adding them by hand it knows which prefix is needed from current browser data.

entry.title: Awesome Ant Design
entry.summary: A resource list for Ant Design, the enterprise-class UI design language. Unlike Material UI, its components target data-heavy enterprise interfaces; the list gathers community components and templates.

entry.title: Awesome CSS
entry.summary: A list gathering the CSS language, tools and resources by topic. Unlike learning-focused CSS lists, it also covers frameworks, tooling and methodologies such as BEM.

entry.title: Awesome CSS Learning
entry.summary: A resource list focused on learning the CSS language and its modules — Flexbox, Grid, selectors. Unlike general CSS lists, it picks resources that teach the language itself, not frameworks or tools.

entry.title: Awesome PostCSS
entry.summary: A resource list for PostCSS, the tool that transforms CSS with plugins. Unlike preprocessors such as Sass, every transformation is a separate plugin; the list groups them by purpose.

entry.title: Awesome Tailwind CSS
entry.summary: A list of plugins, components, templates and tools for Tailwind CSS. Unlike the official docs, it collects community-made component kits and helper tools.

entry.title: BuildBootstrap
entry.summary: Builds a Bootstrap layout visually by drag and drop and generates its code. Unlike writing it by hand, you see the grid while you build it; the trade-off is that later customisation is still manual.

entry.title: Bulma
entry.summary: A modern framework built purely from CSS (no JavaScript), based on Flexbox. Unlike Bootstrap it ships no JS components — you take the classes and write your own interactions.

entry.title: Buttons Generator
entry.summary: Ready CSS button styles with their code for use in projects. Unlike component libraries it adds no dependency — click and copy plain CSS.

entry.title: Cruip
entry.summary: Modern landing-page and UI templates (Tailwind-heavy). Unlike building from scratch you get a ready, coherent page; some are free, the fuller templates are paid.

entry.title: CSS Battle
entry.summary: A game where you reproduce a target image with as little CSS code as possible. Unlike tutorials it sharpens skill through competition and scoring.

entry.title: CSS Formatter
entry.summary: Un-minifies and formats CSS back into a readable shape. Unlike a minifier it expands a compressed file — useful when you need to read someone else’s stylesheet.

entry.title: CSS Layout
entry.summary: Ready CSS recipes for common layouts and components (cards, centring, sticky header). Unlike searching it gives each pattern as a copyable, self-contained example.

entry.title: CSS Media Query Generator
entry.summary: Generates CSS media queries for specific device sizes. Unlike writing them by hand, you pick common device breakpoints from a ready list.

entry.title: CSS Minifier
entry.summary: A simple tool that minifies CSS by stripping whitespace and comments, with an API too. Unlike build-pipeline tools such as cssnano or esbuild, it handles a one-off job with nothing to install.

entry.title: CSS Reference
entry.summary: A reference showing every CSS property with a visual example. Unlike the spec it explains “what does this property do” with a live demo rather than text.

entry.title: cubic-bezier.com
entry.summary: Lea Verou’s tool to craft CSS easing curves by hand and compare them against presets live. Unlike easings.net, you build your own curve by dragging handles rather than picking a preset.

entry.title: Easings.net
entry.summary: Visualises common easing curves and lets you copy the cubic-bezier for each. Unlike cubic-bezier.com, you choose among named presets rather than building a curve.

entry.title: Fancy Border-Radius
entry.summary: A visual tool that generates CSS border-radius for organic shapes. Unlike writing it by hand, you tune the eight-value (slash) syntax by dragging handles.

entry.title: FreeFrontEnd
entry.summary: A large directory of HTML, CSS and JavaScript code samples and tutorials. Unlike searching CodePen, it classifies examples by type — buttons, menus, cards, animation.

entry.title: Layoutit Grid
entry.summary: A tool to draw a CSS Grid layout by drag-and-drop and generate its code. Unlike writing grid by hand you build the row/column structure visually and export it.

entry.title: Material UI
entry.summary: A React component library implementing Google’s Material Design. Unlike Ant Design it follows the Material guidelines closely; the theming system can move you away from that look, but it takes work.

entry.title: NES.css
entry.summary: A CSS framework with a retro 8-bit NES look. Unlike frameworks such as Bootstrap it supplies style, not behaviour: it is CSS only and needs no JavaScript.

entry.title: Neumorphism.io
entry.summary: A tool generating CSS for soft-shadowed “neumorphism” boxes. Unlike writing shadows by hand it lets you tune the dual shadow visually and gives the code.

entry.title: Normalize.css
entry.summary: A small CSS base that evens out default styling differences across browsers. Unlike CSS resets it keeps the useful defaults instead of wiping everything, and fixes only the inconsistencies.

entry.title: Pure.css
entry.summary: A tiny, modular CSS framework of just a few KB (Yahoo). Unlike large frameworks you take only the module you need and keep the page light.

entry.title: uiGradients
entry.summary: A tool that shows ready CSS gradients and gives their code. Unlike mixing colours by hand you pick a pleasing transition and copy it straight.

entry.title: W3C CSS Validator
entry.summary: Validates CSS against the official W3C rules, accepting a URL, a file or pasted text. Unlike linters such as Stylelint, it checks conformance to the standard, not style.

entry.title: CSS-Tricks Snippets
entry.summary: An archive of snippets for CSS, HTML, JavaScript and .htaccess built up over years. Against scattered blog posts each snippet has its own page and discussion — and the comments usually hold a better version.

entry.title: Easing Wizard
entry.summary: A visual builder for CSS easing curves that covers not just cubic-bezier but linear() spring and bounce curves. That linear() support is what dates it past cubic-bezier.com: spring animation in CSS no longer needs a library.

entry.title: Uiverse
entry.summary: A community-contributed gallery of open-source UI elements: buttons, cards, loaders, toggles. Unlike CodePen, everything is MIT-licensed, copy-paste ready and offered as plain CSS or Tailwind, with no framework attached.

entry.title: CSS-Tricks
entry.summary: Two decades of CSS technique, whose Flexbox and Grid guides became widely cited references. Faster than the spec when you are hunting a specific layout problem.

entry.title: Flexbox Froggy
entry.summary: The Flexbox sibling of Grid Garden, teaching alignment by positioning frogs. Unlike reading the docs you see every property’s effect at once — it settles the justify-content versus align-items confusion in twenty minutes.

entry.title: Grid Garden
entry.summary: A 28-level game teaching CSS Grid by watering carrots. Properties like grid-column and grid-area stick when you type them rather than read them.

entry.title: Foundation for Sites
entry.summary: The long-running alternative to Bootstrap: a responsive front-end framework with an XY grid, accessibility-minded components and a separate edition for HTML email. Against Bootstrap it imposes fewer visual opinions — components arrive unstyled and you bring the design. Caveat: the last release was September 2024 and the last push January 2025. The project is not archived, but it has been dormant since then and its marketing site still advertises a webinar from 2017.

entry.title: Bootstrap
entry.summary: Ready components and a grid system that get you a working interface without design decisions. Unlike Tailwind it hands you finished components rather than building blocks; the cost is that a Bootstrap site is recognisable from a distance.

entry.title: Tailwind CSS
entry.summary: You style with utility classes and the build step drops unused ones, so the CSS file stops growing. Unlike Bootstrap it hands you building blocks rather than components — the look is entirely yours.
